To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the elevation of zinc protopophyrin levels in the blood of mice following sublethal doses (0.25 Gy) of whole body irradiations is due to the recovery of the hemopoietic system following radiation-induced injury.
sublethal whole body irradiation of mice elevates blood levels of ZPP 2 to 3 fold over normal levels, and this elevation is not due to iron deficiency or inhibition of ferrochetlase.
whole body irradiation of mice elevates the blood level of ZPP in a manner dependent upon the dose of irradiation, the dose rate, and the hematopoietics status of the animal.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the effects of radiation and lead poisoning on hematopoiesis.
the mechanism of the elevation of ZPP in mice after whole body irradiation and its relationship to recovery of the hematologic system.
the mechanism of elevation of zinc protoprophyrin levels following whole body x-irradiation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the radiation-induced elevation in ZPP levels is a reflection of a recovery of the hematologic system following radiation injury.
the ZPP level is elevated following whole body irradiations in mice.
the elevation of ZPP in irradiated animals is not due to either iron deficiency or inhibition of ferrocheletase, but that it is a consequence of radiation injury to hematopoietic tissue.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ZPP is an indicator of hematopoietic recovery following radiation injury.
the radiation-induced elevation in ZPP may serve as a marker for the recovery of the bone marrow from the effects of whole body irradiations.
radiation-induced elevation of zinc protopophyrin in the blood is a useful indicator of the recovery of the blood forming system following sublethal irradiation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ZPP levels can be elevated in the absence of lead poisoning and/or iron deficiency and may be useful as a biomarker of radiation exposure.
radiation exposure causes a transient elevation of ZPP levels that may serve as a biomarker for radiation exposure and recovery of hematopoiesis.
the ZPP assay should not be used as an indicator of iron deficiency in mice that have received sublethal doses whole body irradiation.
